title: Shopify AI Search: How to Make Your Products Easier for AI Shopping Tools to Understand
excerpt: Buyers increasingly ask in plain language. This is how to make a Shopify catalogue legible to both: accurate titles, complete attributes, honest availability, and a discovery audit you can actually run.
intro: I think about how a customer will find a product in two directions now. The first is the search box they type into. The second is the assistant they might ask instead — a shopping agent that reads a store's data and matches it to what someone describes in plain language. If a customer asks for a lightweight travel stroller that folds small enough for a city car, your store may sell exactly that product — and still lose the sale if the title, attributes and variant data never make it obvious. This guide is about the part of that problem you actually control: *the quality of the product data* behind every listing.

sections.heading: What AI shopping search means for Shopify stores
paragraphs: For a decade, product discovery on the web meant one thing: a search engine crawling pages, a person typing keywords, and a ranked list in between. That loop is not going away, but it is no longer the only way a product gets found. Shopping assistants and *agentic storefronts* read structured product information — titles, options, prices, availability — and match it against a request a human makes in *plain language*.

None of this is hypothetical infrastructure. Shopify's documentation describes [Shopify Catalog](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) and [agentic storefront product discovery](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/agentic-storefronts/products) as part of how products reach these experiences. What I want to be precise about: no merchant can configure a flag that makes a specific AI system recommend a specific product. What a merchant can do is make their catalogue *legible* — so that when a system reads it, the reading is accurate.

That distinction matters because it changes what the work is. You are not guessing at prompts or chasing an unknown ranking algorithm. You are doing something you should be doing anyway: cleaning product data, completing attributes, and keeping variants, prices and stock honest. AI discovery raises the stakes of sloppy data, but it does not invent a new kind of work.

sections.heading: How product discovery differs from traditional keyword search
paragraphs: Keyword search matches text. A customer types "travel stroller" and you get pages that contain those words. The store's job was mostly to make sure the right words appeared on the right pages — which is why so many stores stuff synonyms into titles and meta descriptions.

A natural-language request works differently. "Folds small for a city car" contains no keyword a title will ever contain. A system answering it has to reason over *structured attributes*: the fold dimensions, the weight, the intended use. The closer your data is to a machine-readable record of what the product actually is, the more reliably it can be matched — by search, by filters, by comparison, and by agents.

This is also why the same cleanup helps ordinary customers. The person narrowing a collection by size and colour is doing a smaller version of the same task. The catalogue that answers "what fits a city car" is the catalogue that answers "what fits our family" — whether the question arrives from a search box, a filter drawer, or an assistant.

sections.heading: Which product attributes help shoppers and systems understand a product
paragraphs: Start with the title. A title is the first record a system reads and the first thing a human sees. A useful title names the product, its category, and one or two genuinely distinguishing facts — material, size, compatibility. "Babymore Travel System, 3-in-1, with car seat" tells a system and a shopper something they can match against. "The Ultimate Premium Bundle!" tells them nothing they can act on.

Then the attributes: materials, dimensions, sizes, weight limits, compatibility. This is the difference between a catalogue and a spreadsheet of marketing copy. A travel system that lists its folded dimensions in centimetres and kilograms can be matched to the question "will this fit in a hatchback trunk". A listing that only says "compact and convenient" cannot — *structured attributes are the answer*.

Finally, the variant and data that changes per combination. Variant, price and inventory accuracy is where most catalogues quietly rot. A variant that is sold out but not marked as such, a price that only exists in the listing text, a size that maps to the wrong variant — each one corrupts every system that reads the record, and each one is visible to a customer in a store you have documented, like the [product detail view from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) where the record has to survive the trip from admin to checkout.

Availability is part of the message. A system that recommends a product that is actually unavailable has failed the shopper twice: once with a wrong match, once with a dead end. Keeping stock states honest is a discovery feature, not just an operations detail.

sections.heading: How to review product data in Shopify
paragraphs: The review lives in three places. First, the product editor in the admin: title, description, options, variants, price, inventory. Open ten products at random and check each field against the physical product. Where the product is 6.4 kg, the record should say 6.4 kg, not "lightweight".

Second, the product page itself: what the customer actually sees. Titles and descriptions are sometimes transformed by the theme, price and availability are rendered from live data, and images are pulled from the media library. What you must verify is the *rendered record* — title, specifications, variants, price and availability on the page a buyer reads. The desktop detail page is the honest test.

Third, the structured output the page ships. Product pages emit structured data — the machine-readable summary of name, price, currency and availability. If the rendered page and the structured data disagree, the page has two conflicting records. That problem gets its own guide: [Shopify Product Schema: Fix Structured Data Errors](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors).

A practical rhythm: review a random sample weekly, every product you touch monthly, and the full catalogue quarterly. Catalogue quality is a maintenance practice, the same way [store maintenance](/shopify-store-maintenance) is — not a one-time migration project.

sections.heading: Shopify Catalog, AI channels, and what merchants can control
paragraphs: Shopify is building the infrastructure for products to be discovered through channels a merchant does not operate directly: agentic storefronts, shopping assistants, and other AI-mediated surfaces. [Shopify's documentation on agentic storefront products](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/agentic-storefronts/products) is the primary source for how that product discovery is intended to work, and [the Shopify Catalog write-up](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) explains the catalog layer underneath it.

Here is the honest boundary. Merchants do not configure "AI visibility" the way they configure a channel: there is no per-product toggle, no guaranteed placement, no published ranking. What merchants control is the input: the accuracy, completeness and consistency of their product data. What they do not control is how each downstream system uses it.

I treat that the same way I treat any emerging channel: prepare the record, publish it cleanly, and do not buy certainty that does not exist. If a store's data is accurate enough to serve a customer, it is accurate enough to be *understood* — that is the part worth engineering for.

For stores that need this done at catalogue scale — attributes backfilled, variants normalized, schema verified across thousands of products — that is development work. It is the kind of [Shopify development](/shopify-development) I take on, and it is the kind of work that shows up in the [Commerce Journal](/blogs) when I have something specific to report.

sections.heading: A practical product-discovery audit
paragraphs: Run this as a checklist, not a feeling. Pick a representative sample — say twenty products spanning your best sellers, newest arrivals, and the long tail — and score each one.

Title: does it name the product, its category, and at least one distinguishing fact without filler words? Attributes: are materials, dimensions, weight, size and compatibility present where the product has them? Variants: does every purchasable combination exist as a real variant with its own price and stock state? Availability: do the sold-out, in-stock and low-stock states render correctly on the page? Descriptions: do they add information a machine or a shopper cannot get from the title? Structured data: does the page's product markup match the rendered price, currency and availability?

Write down the failure patterns, not the individual failures. "Folded dimensions missing on most travel systems" is an action; "product 2317 is incomplete" is noise. The patterns become your backfill plan — which is exactly the workflow in [Shopify Product Data Management](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management), the guide on turning ad-hoc cleanup into a repeatable catalogue process.

When the audit says attributes are missing at scale, the fix is not twenty manual edits. It is a standardized attribute set, a bulk update, and a validation pass — the data-governance side of the same problem.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid — and what AI visibility cannot guarantee
paragraphs: Mistake one: keyword-stuffing titles in hopes of matching a machine. The systems that reason over product data reward completeness and accuracy, not density. A title optimized for a search engine in 2015 is a title that is harder to match in 2026.

Mistake two: treating "AI visibility" as a deliverable. I will not promise that a given change makes an assistant recommend a given product, because no one honestly can. I will promise that a clean record removes a whole class of mismatches — wrong attribute, wrong price, phantom stock — that any reader of your data would hit.

Mistake three: optimizing the record but not the storefront. If filters do not work, a shopper still cannot narrow the catalogue by the attributes you carefully filled in. Discovery is a pipeline: data, structured output, filtering, search, and the new AI surfaces all read from the same source. The [collection filters guide](/blogs/shopify-collection-filters-guide) covers the middle of that pipeline.
And the honest frame: *you are not optimizing for a guess*. You are making your catalogue correct — which is useful to every reader of it, known or unknown.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Do I need a special app for AI search? No. The foundation is product data: complete attributes, real variants, honest availability. Apps and AI channels sit on top of that record; none of them compensate for a missing one.

Will Google or an AI assistant rank me better if my data is clean? Clean data removes disqualifiers and mismatches. It is a prerequisite, not a guarantee — indexing and ranking have their own stages, which the [pages-not-indexed guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) walks through for the classic search path.

Is this different from normal SEO? The audience of the data has widened. The work — accurate titles, complete attributes, consistent variants, verifiable structured data — is the same work a careful store has always been doing, now with more readers than a crawler.

takeaway: AI discovery does not ask for new tricks; it asks for a catalogue accurate enough to be read. Complete the record, keep availability honest, and every reader — human, filter, or agent — gets the same right answer.

title: Shopify Product Variants Not Working? A Guide to Large Catalogues and Variant Selection
excerpt: Broken selectors, wrong prices, missing images and phantom stock: a map of how variant selection actually works, a troubleshooting path, and what changes when the catalogue gets large.
intro: A customer selects a colour, chooses a size, and expects the price and product image to update. If the selector breaks — or *silently shows the wrong combination* — the product page stops being a reliable buying tool. "Variants not working" is one of the most common problems I get handed, and the useful thing about it is that *the failure modes are limited and testable*. This guide maps the causes, gives you a troubleshooting path, and explains why large variant catalogues change the way themes behave.

sections.heading: What causes Shopify variant selectors to fail?
paragraphs: A variant selector is a promise: the options the customer picks combine into one purchasable thing, and the page keeps that thing honest. When people report "variants not working", the underlying cause is almost always one of four places: the product data, the theme's selection logic, an app that intercepts the page, or a rendering problem on a large catalogue.

Product data failures are the quiet ones. A variant exists in the admin but never appears as an option on the page because the option mapping is wrong. A size is spelled "L" in one place and "Large" in another, so the selector builds a combination that does not exist. The page looks broken, but the record behind it is the thing that is broken.

Theme failures are the loud ones. The selector updates the price but not the image, or the add-to-cart button still posts the product's first variant. These are logic errors in how the theme reads the selection — and they are exactly the kind of [theme work](/shopify-theme-development) that is fixable once it is correctly diagnosed. The distinction between "the data is wrong" and "the logic is wrong" decides which fix is real, and the [product record note from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) is a good model of the data side: if the record is complete, the page has something to render.

App failures need their own section because they are the hardest to attribute. An inventory sync app, a size-chart app, or a personalization script can all touch the same DOM the theme owns. When a selector works in one environment and not another, an app is usually the variable that changed.

sections.heading: Why selected options, prices, images and stock can become inconsistent
paragraphs: Every time a customer changes a selection, five values on the page must move together: the selected option, the price, the image, the availability state, and the identifier that add-to-cart submits. *The selection state is a contract*, and a broken selector is a contract where one side stopped performing.

The most common inconsistency is the price lag: the selector shows a new selection, the price updates, but the add-to-cart payload still carries the original variant. The customer pays for the wrong thing — or the order arrives wrong — and the bug reads as "checkout is broken" even though checkout is doing exactly what it was told.

The second common one is the image. A variant image is optional; when a selected variant has no image of its own, the page should fall back to the product's primary image. Themes that assume every variant has an image will show a stale or missing picture instead of the fallback — visually broken, technically a missing default.

The third is availability. A selected variant can be sold out while the product as a whole has stock. The page must reflect the *variant's* stock state, not the product's. If it doesn't, customers select a combination they cannot buy, and the error surfaces at checkout — the worst possible place for it to live.

sections.heading: How large variant catalogues change theme behaviour
paragraphs: Most themes are written for the small-catalogue case: a handful of options, a handful of variants, all of them loaded with the product template. That assumption is fine — until a catalogue stops being small. Shopify's [product variant limit is now 2,048 for all merchants](https://shopify.dev/changelog/posts/the-product-variant-limit-is-now-2048-for-all-merchants), and the platform's guidance for [supporting high-variant products](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/product-merchandising/variants/support-high-variant-products) exists precisely because *2,048 is a ceiling, not a target*.

The practical problem: a theme that assumes every variant is loaded into `product.variants` will work at 12 variants and fail at 800. Rendering thousands of hidden option inputs bloats the page. Selection logic that re-scans every variant on every click gets slow. Filters and search that index variants instead of options start returning noise.

Large catalogues also change what "the product" means. A garment line with eight colours and twelve sizes is not twelve products and eight colours — it is one product with 96 purchasable facts. The [travel-system notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-travel-system-details) cover the other side of this: a travel system that is not a single item. Both are the same lesson — the unit of commerce in Shopify is the *variant*, and the page has to treat it that way.

If your catalogue has hundreds of variants per product, the fix is architectural, not a patch: lazy or selective variant loading, option-level logic instead of variant-level loops, and explicit fallbacks. That is a theme change in the real sense — the kind of work [Shopify development](/shopify-development) exists for — and it is worth doing before the next catalogue growth forces it.

sections.heading: How to troubleshoot variant-selection problems
paragraphs: Work top-down: data first, then page, then code. *Test every option combination*, not just the happy path. With two options of three values each, that is nine selections — and the bug is usually in a corner combination nobody orders: the largest size in the colour that is almost sold out.

Then *verify sold-out and unavailable variants*. Select each out-of-stock combination and check three things: the button state, the availability text, and what add-to-cart actually submits. A page that shows "Sold out" but still posts the variant to the cart has a real bug, even if most customers never see it.

Then *check URL parameters, images and add-to-cart behaviour*. A variant selection that survives a page refresh encodes the selection in the URL — if the URL says one variant and the page says another, the page is misreading its own state. Open the network tab on add-to-cart and read the payload: the variant identifier in that request is the only ground truth for what the customer will be charged.
Here is the shape of what you are checking at every selection — the five values that must move together (illustrative structure, not a live store export):

# A selection state lives in the URL and the page at once
/product/example-travel-system?variant=45000000000001

# For every selection change, verify all five stay in sync:
#   selected option(s)   the active combination
#   price                that variant's price, never the base price
#   image                the variant image, or the documented fallback
#   availability         that variant's stock state
#   add-to-cart payload  the variant identifier, never the product identifier
sections.codeCaption: THE FIVE VALUES THAT MUST MOVE TOGETHER — ILLUSTRATIVE STRUCTURE, NOT A STORE EXPORT

sections.heading: What developers should know about high-variant products
paragraphs: If you are reading this as the person who fixes the page, the short version: stop assuming `product.variants` contains everything. On a high-variant product it may not, and logic that maps options to variants by scanning the full array is both wrong and slow at scale.

Build selection logic at the option level: the customer's choices define a combination, and the theme resolves that combination to a variant — loading only what it needs. Render option values from the product's options, not from an enumerated list of variants. And make the fallbacks explicit: missing variant image, missing variant price, out-of-stock combination. An explicit fallback is a feature; an implicit assumption is a bug with a long fuse.

Test against the real ceiling's neighbourhood. A catalogue with 900 variants is a different system than one with 90 — load time, selector responsiveness, and filter behaviour all change. If the store cannot produce a 900-variant product for testing, a duplicate with synthetic variants is a legitimate stand-in, clearly labelled as such.

The [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) covers the data side of this — because a high-variant product with inconsistent option values is two bugs wearing one costume.

sections.heading: A regression checklist for variant changes
paragraphs: Variant changes are high-risk because the blast radius is the whole product page. Any change to options, variants, prices or images deserves a written pass — the same discipline the [QA checklists](/resources/shopify-qa-checklist) use for anything customer-facing.

The checklist: every option value renders; every combination resolves to a real variant; price, image and availability update per selection; sold-out combinations disable add-to-cart; the add-to-cart payload carries the correct variant identifier; the selection survives a refresh; and the page still performs at the catalogue's real size. Run it in desktop and mobile, because mobile selectors are often a different implementation wearing the same name.

After the change, watch the signals that say a corner combination broke: the refund question about the wrong size, the support email with the screenshot of a missing image. A variant bug that only appears in one corner of the option grid can run quietly for months — the checklist exists so it never gets that far.

sections.heading: When the issue belongs to a theme, app or product-data setup
paragraphs: The diagnosis splits cleanly once you have run the troubleshooting path. If the admin record is wrong — missing variant, mismatched option values, price on the product but not the variant — *the fix is in the data*, and no theme change will help until the record is correct.

If the record is correct and the page still misbehaves, the fix is in the theme's selection logic. If the page behaves correctly in a clean theme and not in the live one, the fix is in the theme or an app. The clean-theme test is the fastest way to attribute the bug — and it is the first thing I do when a store is handed to me with "variants not working" as the problem statement.

If an app owns part of the behaviour, the fix may be in the app's configuration, in removing the app, or in making the theme and the app stop fighting over the same element. App-conflict bugs are miserable precisely because the fault line is not visible in any single codebase.

Whatever the attribution, the standard is the same: the page must keep its contract with the customer — five values, in sync, on every selection. That is the whole job, and it is why *a variant is a purchasable fact*, and every layer of the page exists to keep that fact visible and correct.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Is the variant limit per product or per store? Per product. Shopify's current allowance is 2,048 variants per product for all merchants — the number that large-catalogue themes must be designed around.

Can an app cause a selector to break? Yes. Inventory, sizing, personalization and upsell apps all touch product-page behaviour. When a selector works on a clean theme and not on the live one, the app layer is the prime suspect.

Do I need a developer for every variant issue? No — many are data fixes, made in the admin in minutes. You need a developer when the theme's selection logic is wrong, when the catalogue's size exceeds the theme's assumptions, or when an app and the theme disagree about who owns the page.

takeaway: A broken variant selector is five values that stopped moving together. Check the data, check the selection state, read the add-to-cart payload — the attribution between data, theme and app falls out of the evidence.

title: Shopify Migration SEO Checklist: How to Move Stores Without Losing Important URLs
excerpt: A migration can look perfect on launch day and still lose the URLs a store spent years earning. The inventory, the map, the redirects, and the post-launch checks — in the order I run them.
intro: A redesign can look perfect on launch day and still create a serious problem if customers, backlinks, or search engines keep arriving at old URLs that no longer work. I have watched migrations where the new store is better in every way except that half the old URLs die silently — and *those are the URLs the store earned*. This guide is the checklist I run before and after a move: inventory, mapping, redirects, and the post-launch verification that tells you what actually made it through.

sections.heading: What can go wrong during a Shopify migration?
paragraphs: The visible store is the easy part. The things that break are the ones nobody sees on launch day: a backlink from a magazine article now hitting a 404, a collection page that ranked for a money keyword now gone, an old product URL that customers bookmarked years ago, a blog post that other sites cite for its fitting advice.

The failure mode is not usually a crash. It is a *silent retirement* — the URL stops existing, nothing tells anyone, and the signal it carried (ranking, backlinks, bookmarks, search impressions) evaporates. A month after launch, the store looks slower and smaller in search than the old one did, and nobody can say when it started.

The second failure mode is the messy redirect: a chain (A to B to C), a redirect to the wrong target, or a 302 used where a 301 was meant. These work "fine" until you need the full signal transferred, and the difference matters — [Shopify's redirect documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/menus-and-links/url-redirect) is the primary reference, and [Google's technical requirements for search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/technical) is what the destination side has to satisfy.
The checklist below exists so that neither failure mode gets a quiet moment. *A redirect is a promise*, and the whole job is making sure every promise is written down before launch and kept after it.

docRefs.title: Creating and managing URL redirects (Shopify)
docRefs.note: Shopify's merchant documentation for creating redirects, importing them, and which path types Shopify can and cannot redirect through.

docRefs.title: Technical requirements for search (Google)
docRefs.note: Google's reference for what destination pages must satisfy — accessible, indexable, with a healthy HTTP response — after a redirect lands on them.

sections.heading: Build a URL inventory before changing the store
paragraphs: Before anything moves, list everything that exists. The inventory has four rows per store: products (with their canonical URLs), collections, pages and blog posts, and — easily forgotten — image and asset URLs that other pages and feeds reference.

The honest source for the inventory is the old site's sitemap, its search-console data, and a crawl. A sitemap tells you what the store declared; a crawl tells you what is reachable; Search Console tells you which of those URLs were actually earning impressions and clicks. *The inventory is the map*, and a map built from the sitemap alone will miss the URLs that only backlinks and bookmarks know about.

For each URL, record what it is, where it points, and — if the data exists — how it performs. That last column is what separates a technical exercise from a business decision: the URL that drives a third of organic orders gets a better destination and more scrutiny than the URL that has not seen a click in two years.

If the store is large, this is the step that gets skipped under deadline pressure, and it is the step that makes every later step guesswork. A store that is [moving through a Shopify development engagement](/shopify-development) should treat the inventory as the first deliverable, because it defines what "done" means at the end.

sections.heading: Map old URLs to the most relevant new destinations
paragraphs: Every old URL gets one of four decisions: a 301 to its best new destination, a 301 to a category or landing page when no single equivalent exists, an intentional 404 when the content is genuinely gone, or a note explaining why it was left alone. The discipline is that *every* URL in the inventory gets a decision — an unmapped URL is not "no problem", it is an unexamined one.

The mapping rule: the destination must be the most relevant page, not the closest page. A renamed product redirects to the renamed product. A discontinued line redirects to the collection that replaced it. A blog post whose content moved gets a redirect to the page that now carries that content. Redirecting everything to the homepage is the classic shortcut, and it is how a migration quietly taxes every URL it touches.

sections.heading: How to create and validate Shopify redirects
paragraphs: Shopify creates redirects from the admin (Settings, or the URL redirects area) and imports them from CSV at scale. One redirect per row, one target per source, and the redirect type said honestly: 301 when the old page is retired and the signal should move, 302 when the move is temporary.

The validation step is where the plan meets reality. For a sample of the mapping — and for every URL that mattered in the inventory — request the old URL and read the response: a single 301, straight to the final destination, ending in a 200. A chain of two or three hops is a bug in the plan even if the browser never complains; chains dilute the signal and they rot.

Also check what Shopify cannot redirect cleanly. Some path types behave differently — the platform's own [redirect documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/menus-and-links/url-redirect) lists which URL types can be redirected and how — so the plan must know which rows are platform-supported and which need a different mechanism, such as handling at the domain or CDN layer.

After import, re-crawl the old URLs. The crawl result is the evidence: every mapped URL resolving to one hop and a live destination is the checklist row that gets ticked. *301 is a transfer, not a copy* — the old page's standing moves only if the redirect is clean and the destination is healthy.

sections.heading: Product, collection, blog and image URL checks
paragraphs: Products: the new product's URL should be the stable one the store intends to keep. If the handle changed, the old handle gets a redirect. If the product moved between collections, the product URL itself should not have changed — that is a collection problem, not a product one.

Collections: a renamed or restructured collection is one of the highest-value redirect rows in the plan, because collections are often the URLs that earn category search traffic. The [collection SEO notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo) cover why the collection itself — not just the products in it — is the SEO surface, which is exactly why its URL deserves the best destination available.

Blog posts: the posts that other sites link to get individual redirects to their new homes. Posts whose content was merged get a redirect to the merged page. A blog that is being shut down entirely still needs its top posts mapped — those are the URLs with backlinks on them.

Images: the most neglected row. Old image URLs referenced by backlinks, feeds, or pages that were not updated will 404 unless the assets moved with their paths. The check is simple: request a sample of old image URLs and confirm they resolve. Image URLs that die are how a migration leaks broken layouts onto other people's pages.

sections.heading: What to test before DNS changes and launch
paragraphs: The pre-launch pass runs on the new store while it is still behind the old DNS: every redirect row tested (sample plus all high-value rows), every key page on the new store checked for a 200, a canonical tag, and the content it should have, and the new sitemap published and complete.

Then the cross-checks: the new store's internal links point to new URLs (no stale links to old handles), the search and filter URLs work, and checkout completes an order on the new store. *Launch day is a checkpoint, not a finish line* — the switch itself is the boring part, and the verification after it is where the migration is actually won or lost.

One more pre-launch check that is specific to migrations: the new store's pages must be eligible for indexing on their own. Redirects do not fix a destination that is blocked, canonicalized to the wrong host, or thin. If the old store's URL is redirected to a new page that Google cannot or will not index, the signal has nowhere to land — which is the failure mode the [pages-not-indexed guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) walks through step by step.

Structured data needs the same attention: product and page markup must be correct on the new URLs *before* launch, so the first crawl of the new store sees consistent data. The [product schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) is the reference for that pass — doing it post-launch is doing it with a backlog of mismatches already accumulating.

sections.heading: Post-launch monitoring in Google Search Console
paragraphs: The Search Console property for the migrating domain is the owner's to connect and read — it is where the after-evidence lives, and it is the one step in this checklist I do not perform on the owner's behalf. Here is what I would look for, and when.

In the first two weeks: the URL inspection results for the high-value redirects — old URL inspected shows the redirect, destination inspected shows it is indexed or a valid candidate. The coverage report will show the new URLs arriving; the old URLs should show up as redirected, not as errors with nothing behind them.

In the first month: impressions and clicks for the pages that mattered. The honest expectation is that numbers dip and recover — a migration is a controlled shock, and the recovery curve is the metric of success. A URL that ranked before launch and never recovers is a row in the inventory that needs a second look at its destination.

And the standing habit: keep the Search Console data as the living audit of the redirect plan. Three months after launch, the URLs that are still failing are the ones the plan got wrong — and they are cheap to fix while the mapping is still fresh.

sections.heading: Common redirect mistakes and recovery steps
paragraphs: Mistake one: redirect chains and loops. A redirect that points to another old URL, or two URLs redirecting at each other. Recovery: flatten every chain to a single hop; the crawl re-check finds any that remain.

Mistake two: the 302 that was meant to be a 301. Temporary redirects during staging that never got switched. Recovery: audit the redirect table for 302s older than the launch and decide each one deliberately — flip it or retire it.

Mistake three: the homepage catch-all. Every unmapped URL landing on the homepage, diluting it and burying the real destinations. Recovery: go back through the inventory and give the unmapped rows real decisions, even if the decision is a deliberate 404.

Mistake four: the destination that was never checked. The redirect is perfect and the page it points to is thin, blocked, or canonicalized away. Recovery: fix the destination — *the promise is only as good as the page that keeps it*. A migration done well is not a store that launches; it is a store whose old URLs still work, on purpose, forever after.

takeaway: The store that survives a migration is not the one with the best launch day — it is the one whose inventory was complete, whose redirects were single-hop, and whose destinations were verified after the switch.
seoTitle: Shopify Migration SEO Checklist: Redirects and Launch Checks
seoDescription: Moving to Shopify? Use this migration SEO checklist to map URLs, plan redirects, check important pages and monitor technical issues after launch.

title: Shopify Markets SEO: Languages, Currencies, Hreflang and Duplicate URLs
excerpt: A wrong-currency product page is a translation problem and a configuration problem at once. How Markets organizes international storefronts, what hreflang actually does, and the audit before launch.
intro: If a customer in France lands on an English product page with the wrong currency, the issue is bigger than translation. The store needs to communicate which version belongs to which market — *to people and to search engines*. I write about this one because international stores are where configuration errors become customer-facing errors fast: the wrong price shown is the wrong price sold. This guide is how Shopify Markets is meant to work, where the seams are, and the audit I run before a market goes live.

sections.heading: How Shopify Markets organizes international storefronts
paragraphs: Markets is Shopify's model for selling to different countries and language groups from one store: each market carries its own currency, shipping zones, payment methods, and — for SEO — its own URL structure and language. One catalogue, many storefronts, each with a clear identity.

The SEO-relevant part is that Shopify generates the international signals for you when configured properly: market-specific URLs, canonical tags that point each market version at itself, and [hreflang annotations](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/seo/hreflang) that tell search engines which language and region a page serves. [Shopify's own international SEO documentation for Markets](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/markets/seo) is the primary reference for how these pieces are intended to fit together.

The phrase that matters is "when configured properly". Markets removes most of the manual work, but it does not remove the failure modes: a market that exists in the shipping settings but not the URL structure, a language selector that writes one state while the page says another, or a theme that renders extra hreflang tags on top of the platform's own. *The platform generates the signals; the configuration decides whether they agree*.

docRefs.title: International SEO for Markets (Shopify)
docRefs.note: Shopify's merchant documentation for how Markets handles hreflang, canonical URLs and market-specific sitemaps — the first stop for the intended behaviour.

docRefs.title: Hreflang (Shopify theme developer docs)
docRefs.note: The developer-side reference for how hreflang tags are emitted on theme pages, including what a theme can and cannot change.

sections.heading: Subfolders vs. subdomains vs. country-code domains
paragraphs: The URL question — shop.example.com/fr/, example.com/fr/, or example.fr — is a decision with real consequences, and it is the one merchants most want to reverse after launch.

Subfolders under the primary domain are the pattern Shopify's Markets is built around, and the one with the least moving parts: one domain, one set of sitemaps per market (or one consolidated sitemap with market URLs), and canonicals that stay on one host. For most stores, subfolders are the right default, and they are what the platform's tooling assumes.

Subdomains and country-code domains carry their own weight: separate DNS, sometimes separate Search Console properties, separate analytics views, and more places for the configuration to drift. If a store already lives on ccdoms for brand reasons, that is a defensible choice — but then every market's signals (canonical, hreflang, sitemap, robots) must be verified per host, because the platform's defaults stop covering you.

My honest advice: choose the structure before the first market launch, not after. Changing it later is a [migration](/blogs/shopify-migration-seo-checklist) in disguise — every old market URL becomes a redirect row, and every signal has to be rebuilt.

sections.heading: What hreflang does — and what it does not do
paragraphs: Hreflang is a recommendation, not a command. It tells a search engine: these pages serve the same content to different languages and regions — here is the mapping. When the mapping is correct and consistent (page A in French points to page B in English, and page B points back to page A), search engines can serve the right version to the right user.

What it does not do: it does not create the versions, it does not translate content, it does not guarantee any ranking, and — this is the big one — *it does not fix inconsistent pages*. If the French page and the English page have different prices, different availability, or different content, hreflang is annotating a discrepancy rather than resolving it.

The symmetry requirement is where most implementations break. Hreflang is a graph: every tag you emit is a promise that the target page points back. A one-way annotation is a half-promise, and search engines treat broken mappings as noise. The audit below checks symmetry explicitly, because it is the check that catches the most real-world damage.

sections.heading: Canonical URLs across translated product pages
paragraphs: Every market version of a product page should canonicalize to itself — to the URL in the market it belongs to. The failure mode is the accidental cross-canonical: the French product page carrying a canonical that points at the English one, telling search engines the French page is a duplicate that should be discarded.

This failure is usually a configuration or theme problem, not a content problem. A market that is missing from the URL structure produces pages the platform cannot canonicalize correctly. A theme that hardcodes a canonical to the primary market overwrites the platform's own output. *A wrong canonical is a silent retirement* — the page keeps loading, keeps selling, and keeps telling search engines it does not exist.

The check is two lines per page: read the canonical tag in the page source, and confirm it equals the page's own URL in its own market. Run it across a sample of products in every market before launch, and re-run it after any theme or market change. It is cheap, it is deterministic, and it catches the most expensive class of international bug.

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr-fr" href="https://shop.example.com/fr/products/example-chair" />

<!-- English product page -->

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en"    href="https://shop.example.com/en/products/example-chair" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr-fr" href="https://shop.example.com/fr/products/example-chair" />

sections.heading: How localized content differs from direct translation
paragraphs: A translated product title is a start, not a finish. Localization means the page answers the market's question in that market's terms: units (kilograms, not pounds), sizes (the EU scale, not US), legal phrases, payment expectations, and the vocabulary that market actually searches for.

The SEO-visible difference: a direct translation keeps the source market's keywords, which the target market may never type. A localized page uses the phrasing that market's searchers use — which is why the page earns impressions instead of being a perfect translation nobody finds.

And the honest boundary: I do not translate. Localization is a content decision the store makes with someone who knows the market; my part is making sure the technical layer — URLs, canonicals, hreflang, sitemaps — does not undermine the content once it is written. A beautifully localized page on a broken hreflang graph is a beautiful page search engines cannot place.

For stores selling to multiple markets, this is also where the [collection-level SEO work](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo) has to happen per market: a collection that works in English may need a different structure, or a different name, to work in French.

sections.heading: How to audit market URLs, currencies and language selectors
paragraphs: The audit runs per market, and it has a fixed order. First, the URL: load the market's homepage and a sample of products, and confirm the URL is the market's own (not the primary market's with a query parameter doing the work). Second, the currency: confirm the displayed currency matches the market's configured currency — and that the currency selector, when used, lands on the market's own URLs rather than a session-only switch.

Third, the language selector: pick a market in the selector, and verify the URL changes to the market's structure. A selector that changes the page without changing the URL is the classic red flag — the customer sees French, the page is still the English URL, and every signal says English.

Fourth, the tags: canonical self-referencing in each market, hreflang present and symmetric, and the market's pages in the sitemap. Fifth, the data: prices and availability rendered per market. *The audit is a set of deterministic checks*, which is what makes it repeatable — run it before launch, after every theme deploy, and whenever a market's configuration changes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes, including duplicate hreflang output
paragraphs: Mistake one: the double-emitted hreflang. A theme (or an app, or a snippet someone added in 2024) renders its own hreflang tags on top of the platform's. Two sets of annotations on one page is contradictory noise, and it is the mistake I see most often in international audits. The fix is finding every emitter and leaving exactly one — usually the platform's.

Mistake two: the market that exists in shipping but not in SEO. The market ships and sells, but its URLs were never part of the structure — so its pages are the primary market's pages with a currency override. The fix is configuring the market's URL structure and re-running the canonical check.
Mistake three: the broken symmetry. Half the hreflang graph points one way. The fix is the symmetry check across a product sample in every market pair — mechanical, and decisive.

Mistake four: auditing the primary market only. The primary market is configured first and configured best; every other market is where the drift lives. If the audit covered one market, it covered the easiest one. *The other markets are the store*.

sections.heading: International SEO launch checklist
paragraphs: Before a market goes live, in order: the market's URL structure configured and loading its own pages; canonical tags self-referencing in that market; hreflang present, symmetric, single-emitted; the market's pages in the sitemap; currency and price rendering verified on a product sample; the language selector landing on market URLs; and the content decision documented — which pages are localized, which are translated, which are intentionally the primary-market version.

After launch: the Search Console property(s) for the relevant domain, checking that the market's URLs are being crawled and indexed. *Indexing is its own stage* — a correctly configured market whose URLs never get indexed is a configuration problem that looks like an SEO problem, and the [pages-not-indexed guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) is where that diagnosis runs.

The standing habit: one market's worth of the audit per quarter, rotating through the markets, so no market's drift gets older than a quarter. International stores fail slowly — one wrong canonical at a time — and the rotation is what keeps the failure from becoming the default.

takeaway: Hreflang is a graph of promises between versions of the same page. Verify the promises — canonical self-reference, symmetric annotations, one emitter, market-owned URLs — and the international store stops fighting its own configuration.
seoTitle: Shopify Markets SEO: Hreflang and International URLs
seoDescription: Learn how Shopify Markets handles international SEO, language URLs, hreflang, canonicals and localized content—and what to check before launch.

title: Shopify Product Schema Errors: How to Check Price, Availability and Product Data
excerpt: When the page shows one price and the markup says another, the search systems reading that page have two conflicting records. How to inspect, validate and fix product structured data without adding a second schema on top.
intro: You have updated a product's price and stock status in Shopify, but the page's structured data still shows something different. That mismatch undermines the consistency of the information search systems receive — and it is one of the most checkable problems in storefront SEO, because the evidence is on the page itself. This guide is the diagnostic path: what the markup is supposed to say, how to read what actually shipped, and how to fix the mismatch *without adding a second schema on top*.

sections.heading: What product structured data communicates
paragraphs: Product structured data is the machine-readable summary a product page ships with: the product's name, its price, the currency, its availability, and which offer those values belong to. Search systems read it as the page's own account of what is for sale, at what price, and whether it can be bought right now.

The word to hold onto is *summary*. The markup is not a source of truth — it is a rendering of the truth, generated from the product's live data. When the summary disagrees with the page a customer reads, the page has *two conflicting records*, and every system that reads the markup inherits the discrepancy.

This is why schema problems are fixable in a way that most SEO problems are not: the check is deterministic. Read the rendered price, read the markup's price, compare. Read the availability, read the markup's availability, compare. A mismatch is a bug with a location, and the job is finding which layer produced the wrong value.

sections.heading: Product, Offer, price, currency and availability
paragraphs: The shape that matters is the relationship: a Product holds an Offer, the Offer carries the price, the price carries a currency, and the availability states whether the offer can be acted on right now. Get any of those wrong and the summary is wrong in a specific, checkable way.

The currency is the one that gets skipped. A price without a currency, or with the wrong one, is a number a system cannot safely use — and on a store selling to several markets, the wrong currency is the international version of the same bug. The [Markets guide](/blogs/shopify-markets-international-seo) covers the market structure; this is where it becomes a data problem.

Availability has the same shape: a state, not a label. In stock, out of stock, preorder, sold out — the markup should carry the state the page is showing. *The sale price is a state, not a label*: a discounted product that no longer has a sale still carrying a sale price in its markup is a mismatch that survives until someone checks.
Here is the shape of a correct product record — illustrative values, the structure is the point:
sections.codeCaption: THE RECORD, AS IT SHOULD READ — ILLUSTRATIVE VALUES

sections.heading: Why Shopify themes and apps can produce conflicting markup
paragraphs: Three layers can touch the product markup, and any one of them can produce a wrong value. The theme renders the page and often emits the schema. An app can inject its own product markup — reviews, subscription, size charts — and occasionally injects a second, stale product block. And the product data itself changes: a price updated in the admin, a sale that started and ended, a variant that went out of stock.

The classic failure is staleness at the seam: the theme's schema is generated once from the data it had when it rendered, and the price changed after that. Or the app's block was written for last year's data shape and quietly emits the old price. *The rendered page is the source of truth* — the markup's job is to match it, and when it does not, one of the three layers drifted.

A second classic is duplication: two product blocks on one page, one from the theme and one from an app, with different values. A system reading that page encounters two answers and picks the one it parses first — which is not a strategy you can rely on. The [Merchant Center guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) covers the downstream version of this problem, where the feed and the page disagree and the shopping channel has to pick a side.

sections.heading: How to inspect rendered HTML and JSON-LD
paragraphs: The inspection takes two minutes per product and settles the diagnosis. Open the product page, open the page source, and find the structured data — the JSON-LD script blocks in the head, or the microdata in the body. Read the Product block: name, price, currency, availability, and the offer's URL.

Then read the page the customer sees: the title, the price, the currency symbol, the availability state, the add-to-cart button. Compare field by field. A mismatch now has a location — a specific value on a specific layer — and the fix starts from evidence instead of suspicion.

The same pass works for what customers do not see but search systems do: the page's title tag, its canonical, and the image references inside the markup. Google's [structured data guidance for merchants](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7331077) sets the standard for what the data must agree with, and its [image documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) covers the image side — discoverable image elements, useful alt text, and the context the image sits in.

Do this on a sample that includes the edge cases: the product mid-sale, the product with a sold-out variant, the product that changed price this week. The middle of the catalogue is where the schema is boring; the edges are where it lies.

docRefs.note: Google's reference for what product structured data must agree with — price, availability and identifiers matching the landing page.

docRefs.title: Google Images best practices (Google for Developers)
docRefs.note: The guidance on discoverable image elements, useful alt text and page context — the image half of the product record.

sections.heading: Test variant URLs and sale-price changes
paragraphs: The base product page is the easy case. The test that catches real bugs is the variant URL: load a specific variant and check that the markup's offer matches that variant's price and availability, not the product's first variant. A page that always reports the first variant's price is a bug that only shows up in the combinations customers actually buy.

Then the sale test: start a sale on a test product, read the markup, end the sale, read it again. The markup should move with the state — sale price while the sale is live, regular price after. A store whose markup lags its own sales cycles is feeding stale numbers to every reader of its pages, and the lag is the measurement you need to fix.

The third test is the stock flip: take a variant out of stock, reload, check the availability in the markup; put it back, reload, check again. Availability that does not move with reality is the mismatch that ends in customers ordering what cannot ship — a schema problem that became a fulfilment problem.

None of these tests need special tooling. A browser, the page source, and a product you are willing to change are the whole setup. That is the point: *the check is deterministic*, and a deterministic check is a check you can repeat on every deploy.

sections.heading: Validate structured data and Merchant Center feeds
paragraphs: Once the rendered page and the markup agree, the second audience is the shopping channels. Merchant Center reads both the feed your store publishes and the page's structured data, and its diagnostics flag where they disagree — which makes it the best independent witness to the problem, because it is a system you do not operate checking your work.

The feed and the page are two renderings of the same record, and they can drift: the feed generated daily, the page rendered live, and a price change that lands between the two. When the diagnostics flag a price or availability mismatch, the question is not which side is wrong — it is *which side is stale*, and the fix is making the generation and the rendering read the same source at the same time.

I do not connect a store's Merchant Center on the owner's behalf, and the diagnostics are the owner's to read — but the reading is specific: note the flagged field, the flagged product, and the two values, then run the inspection above on that product. The diagnostic tells you where to look; the page source tells you what is true. The [Merchant Center errors guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) is the full workflow for that loop.

sections.heading: Fix mismatches without adding duplicate schema
paragraphs: The instinct when a product page's schema looks wrong is to add a corrected block alongside it — a second JSON-LD with the right values. That is how one product page ends up with two Product blocks and a system that reads whichever it parses first. *One schema, one truth*: the fix is correcting the emitter, not adding a rival.

So the fix order matters. Find the layer that produces the wrong value — the theme's schema generation, an app's injected block, or a data problem upstream — and fix it there. If an app owns the markup, the fix is the app's configuration or the app itself. If the theme owns it, the fix is the template that generates the block. Adding a patch block on top is a fix that creates the next bug.

When the markup is correct but sparse — no images, no reviews, no brand — the honest move is to fill the record, not to overclaim. A product schema that says exactly what the page says, and says it once, is worth more than a richer schema that disagrees with the page in one field. The trust in the record is the point: *the markup is the page's word*, and a page that keeps its word is a page search systems can rely on.

sections.heading: A repeatable product-schema QA checklist
paragraphs: The checklist is the variant of the inspection above, written down so it survives the deploy that would otherwise re-break it. For a sample of products including the edge cases: price matches, currency matches, availability matches, the offer URL is the product's own URL, the variant URL reports the variant's values, the sale state moves with the sale, and there is exactly one Product block on the page.

Run it after any change that touches prices, inventory, themes, or product apps — because those are the changes that move the data under a static schema. A store with the habit in place finds the mismatch on the deploy that introduced it; a store without it finds it in the Merchant Center diagnostics a month later, at which point the deploy is a memory.

The data underneath deserves the same treatment: if the admin record itself is inconsistent — a price in two places, an availability that does not match the stock — no schema can fix it, because the schema is faithfully reporting a broken record. That is the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management), and it is where this checklist points when the answer is "the data, not the markup". For the stores where the schema layer needs real engineering — a theme that generates the block wrong, an app that needs replacing — that is [development work](/shopify-development), and it is the kind of work with a verifiable before and after: the page and its markup, agreeing.

takeaway: Product schema is the page's word to the machines that read it. The check is deterministic — rendered value versus markup value — and the fix is correcting the emitter, never adding a rival block.

title: Shopify Collection Filters Not Working? A Guide to Search, Sorting and Product Discovery
excerpt: Filters are where catalogue data quality becomes visible: every inconsistent attribute is a filter that fails. How filters should behave, why they go empty or wrong, and the QA pass that keeps them honest.
intro: A customer knows the colour, size or price range they want. If the collection page makes them scroll through every product — or a filter returns the wrong results — the store makes an easy decision feel unnecessarily difficult. Filters are where the catalogue's data quality becomes visible: *every inconsistent attribute is a filter that fails*. This guide covers how filters should behave, why they go missing, empty or wrong, and the QA pass that keeps them honest — on desktop and in the mobile drawer where most of the filtering actually happens.

sections.heading: How collection filters should work
paragraphs: A filter is a promise about the data: if you select "Navy", every product shown has a colour that is genuinely Navy — recorded in the catalogue, not guessed by the page. The customer's mental model is simple and correct; the store's job is to make the model true.

The behaviour contract has four parts. The options shown must match what the catalogue actually contains — no option for a size nobody sells, and no product hiding behind an option that is not offered. The results must respond: selecting a filter changes the grid, the count updates, and the combination of filters narrows correctly. The selected state must be visible: the customer can see what is applied. And the escape must be one action away: a reset that clears the state without losing the customer's place in the store.

*The filter is a promise about the data*, and that is the whole reason filter bugs are rarely filter bugs. When a filter returns the wrong products, the filter is doing exactly what it was told to do with a catalogue that says something different from the truth. The fix is usually the data, not the mechanism — which is also what makes it worth fixing properly.

sections.heading: Filters vs. sorting vs. on-site search
paragraphs: The three discovery tools do different jobs, and stores that blur them confuse customers. Filtering narrows by attribute: colour, size, price band, material. Sorting orders by a dimension: newest, price, best selling. Search answers a question in the customer's words, which may not map to any attribute at all.

The failure mode is overlap without coordination. A customer searches "navy", gets a results page with no filters, and is back at square one — the search found the colour but the page cannot narrow it. Or the filter offers "Navy" as a colour and the search treats "navy" as a free-text match against titles — two different answers to the same question, from the same store.

The coordination is a data decision: the attributes that power the filters are the same attributes the search indexes, and both read from the same catalogue records. *Discovery is one pipeline* — attributes in, results out — and the three tools are three views of it. The [AI discovery guide](/blogs/shopify-ai-search-product-discovery) makes the same point from the other direction: the cleaner the attributes, the more tools can read them correctly.

sections.heading: Why filters can be missing, empty or inaccurate
paragraphs: Missing filters: the attribute exists in the data but not in the filter configuration. A catalogue full of materials that the collection page never offers as a filter. The check is to compare the attributes the products carry against the options the page exposes — the gap is the missing filter, and closing it is a configuration decision, not a code change.

Empty filters: the option exists but selects nothing — or selects the wrong things. This is the data-inconsistency signature. "Navy", "Navy Blue", "Dark Navy" and "navy" are four values to the filter engine and one colour to the customer; a filter built on the raw values has five options, one of which is empty. *The empty option is the audit finding* — it is the catalogue telling you, in the store's own UI, that the data is not standardized.

Inaccurate filters: the option selects products that do not carry the attribute, or misses ones that do. The causes: the attribute was entered in free text instead of the controlled field, the metafield is set on some products and not others, or an app is mapping the attribute its own way. Each cause points at a different layer — the data entry, the field definition, or the app — and the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) is where those layers get sorted out properly.

And the honest note for stores that have lived with this: filter problems are not a reason to remove filtering. A collection that cannot be narrowed is a collection that makes every customer do the store's job. The [navigation notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-navigation) cover the structure that brings customers to the collection; the filters are what make the collection do its job once they are there.

sections.heading: Product tags, metafields and consistent product attributes
paragraphs: The mechanism question is usually the wrong first question. The right first question is: where does the attribute live? The three answers carry different weight. Product options and their values are the platform's structured fields — a size is a value of the Size option, and the filter reads them directly.

Tags are the flexible-but-loose option: free-form, untyped, and only as consistent as the person who typed them. Tags power many filter setups, and they rot in the way tags rot — one person's "navy" is another's "Navy Blue". If the store's filtering rides on tags, the standardization work in the [product data guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) is the prerequisite, not the follow-up.

Metafields and metaobjects are the structured escape: a defined field with a type and, where needed, a controlled set of values — the catalogue's own vocabulary, enforced by the field rather than by discipline. For attributes the store cares about — material, compatibility, care instructions — a metaobject is the difference between "filters work because nobody typed it wrong yet" and "filters work because the field cannot be typed wrong".

The decision rule I use: if the attribute powers a filter, a comparison, or a feed, it deserves a structured field. If it is a label for the team, a tag is fine. The catalogue's job is to be readable by machines — *filters are the most visible reader it has*.

sections.heading: Configure and test Shopify Search & Discovery
paragraphs: Shopify's [Search & Discovery app](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/search-and-discovery) is where the store configures what the search and the filters actually see: which fields are searchable, which attributes become filter facets, and how the results respond. The configuration is the contract between the catalogue and the discovery layer — and like all contracts, it is worth reading in full before you are surprised by it.

The test is behavioural, not configurational. Pick ten products across the catalogue's range and verify each one: it appears under every filter it should satisfy, it does not appear under the ones it should not, and the combination of two filters narrows to the intersection. The store's own collection pages are the test bench — the desktop listing is the first view, and a second storefront's listing shows what the same configuration looks like against a different catalogue shape.

Performance belongs in the test too, because a filter that takes two seconds to respond is a filter customers stop using. Shopify's [theme performance guidance](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/best-practices/performance) is the reference for why filtering on large collections is a theme-side cost, not just a configuration — and why the fix sometimes belongs in the theme rather than the app settings.

When the configuration is right and the behaviour is still wrong, the attribution is usually upstream: the data the configuration reads. That is the pattern across this whole guide, and it is the reason the [Shopify development](/shopify-development) work on discovery is a data project with a UI, not a UI project with data.

docRefs.note: The developer reference for keeping theme interactions — filtering included — fast on large collections.

sections.heading: Mobile filter drawers, selected states and reset controls
paragraphs: Most of a store's filtering happens in a drawer on a phone, and the drawer is a different implementation from the desktop sidebar — same contract, different surface. The test path is the same (does selecting narrow correctly?), but the failure modes are mobile-specific: the drawer that does not show the selected state, the grid that does not update behind the drawer, the count that updates one selection late.

*Selected state is UX*. A customer who cannot see which filters are applied is navigating blind — they select "Navy", the grid changes, they select "Under $100", and the grid changes again, with no record of what they have done. The applied filters must be visible at a glance: as chips above the grid, or as marked options in the drawer. The mobile view of a product's own store is the quickest way to see whether your store keeps that record — the [product detail note from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) is the desktop story; this is where the mobile version earns its keep.

*Reset is a first-class action*. The customer who has filtered themselves into a dead end — Navy + Under $50 + in the discontinued line — needs one tap back to the full collection. A reset that only clears some filters, or a reset that also leaves the collection page itself, is a small frustration that compounds: the customer learns the filters are unreliable, and starts scrolling instead.

The mobile drawer also has a layout job: the options must be tappable, the long attribute values must wrap or truncate sensibly, and the drawer must not trap the customer's scroll. None of this is glamorous, and all of it is the difference between a drawer customers use and a drawer they give up on.

sections.heading: When filter URLs should — and should not — be indexable
paragraphs: A filtered collection often has its own URL — the filter state encoded in the query string. That URL raises a question the unfiltered page never does: should search engines index it? *Indexable is a decision*, not a default, and the decision has real consequences.

The case for indexing: a filter that represents a genuinely distinct, well-stocked view — "all travel systems under $800" — is a page a customer might want to land on, and a search engine might reasonably rank. The case against: the combinatorial explosion. Twelve filters of four values each is 4,096 URLs, most of them thin, most of them near-duplicates of each other, most of them a filter state no customer asked for. Indexed, they dilute the store's crawl budget and create a long tail of low-value pages that the [indexing guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) would spend its whole diagnosis explaining.

The rule I apply: the base collection page is the indexable unit. A filter view is indexable only if it is curated — a real, maintained, well-stocked view the store would stand behind as a page — and even then, the store should say so deliberately, not by accident of the URL structure. The uncurated filter states get told not to be indexed, which is not hiding anything: it is telling search engines the collection page is the page.

This is the same discipline as the [collection SEO notes](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo): the collection is the SEO surface, and every derivative view either earns its own standing or defers to it.

sections.heading: Collection-filter QA checklist
paragraphs: The checklist runs per collection, in order, and it ends with the data. First, the options: every filter offered is populated, every option has results, and no option is an empty promise. Second, the narrowing: a single filter changes the grid correctly; two filters intersect correctly; the count matches the grid.

Third, the state: the selected filters are visible on desktop and in the mobile drawer; the reset clears everything in one action and keeps the customer on the collection. Fourth, the edge cases: a filter that matches one product, a filter combined with a price sort, a filter applied then a new product added to the collection — does the new product appear, and under the right options?

Fifth, the performance: the filter responds without a visible pause on the collection's real size, on the store's real hardware — a mid-range phone on cellular, not a studio laptop on fibre. Sixth, the data: pick the three most-filtered attributes and check how consistently they are recorded across a sample of the catalogue. *The checklist ends where the guide starts* — with the record, because the record is what the promise is made on.

And the habit: run the checklist after any catalogue import, any attribute change, and any theme deploy — the three events that move the data under a working filter. A store that treats filtering as configured-and-done is a store that will discover, from its customers' impatience, that the filters were never done at all.

takeaway: A filter is the catalogue's word made interactive. The options must match the data, the state must stay visible, the reset must be one tap, and the data must be standardized enough that the word is true.
